Having extracted the first three [syllables] of Parā, and then again the group of eight beginning with Aghorī from the Vidyā according to the division of its parts, one should then take the five limbs of that [Vidyā]. ||21||

And by worshipping the world-protectors, O Queen of the Gods, one shall then attain accomplishment; when the mantras have been extracted, accomplishment follows thereafter—of this there is no doubt. ||22||
One should then imagine that *bindu* as the right calf; that very same right calf is [the letter] *va*, the fourth of the row of teeth. (23)

Having placed his right knee [on the ground], the knower of the ritual procedure should apply the trident-staff, which has its base formed by the trident-staff, to the life-force (prāṇa) adorned by the nose.
Then, the heart-mantra joined with the visarga, again the solitary [mantra], the trident-staff, and likewise the hip. ||25||
O Goddess, the fourth tooth is joined with the right shank; thereafter, the trident-handle is said to be as previously described. ||26||
Adorned with an ornament situated at the right ear, one should thereafter extract the *prāṇa* conjoined with the *bindu*. ||27||

In the same manner, the mantra-practitioner should sequentially place the shank resting on the path of the watch (yāma); then the fourth tooth, and then again the staff of the trident (śūladaṇḍa). ||28||
Furthermore, having applied the trident-staff adorned with the left ear, one should subsequently place the right knee upon the syllable of the heart. (29)

Then, indeed, one should place the vital breath (prāṇa) with the visarga, preceded by the letter *da*; then again the staff of the trident (*śūladaṇḍa*), and immediately after that the hip (*nitamba*). ||30||
The wise practitioner should then place a second tooth, adorned with an ornament situated upon the right ear, together with the tongue.
Then, having placed the right shoulder-tip in sequence against the nose, one should likewise place the hip alone and then the shoulder-tip again.
The wise man should raise up his abdomen, and immediately thereafter, listen solely to the *Mālinīvijayottara*. 47b.

The supreme-non-supreme, the non-supreme-supreme, the supreme, and the supreme practitioner—these are the practitioners. From the supreme and so forth, the group of eight beginning with Aghorī, the eight of Aghorī, the group of eight belonging to Aghorī; from the words of the supreme Vidyā, having extracted the protectors from the protectors, and having extracted them, one should join the *bindu* to the *bindu*, row to row. The trident-base, the staff of the trident, the staff of the base; the nose, the door, the heart, the staff of the heart, the staffs; situated in the right ear, in the right ear indeed, the shank, situated in the shank, *stām* joined, joined. The fourth, the fourth, the base of the trident; then from there, the base of the trident, to the right, to the right, the tooth, the tooth, the defiler; situated in the place of the base of the trident, the wise man should extract *u* at the place, the place. The wise man should place it joined with the right knee. 33.
Having extracted the throat itself and the hips in their natural form, the heart joined with the tongue, and the mouth alone; ||34||
Thereafter, one should place the vital breath (prāṇa) upon the right knee-circle; first, however, one should join it to the shaft of the trident, which is adorned with earrings.
Having performed that twice, the mantra-practitioner should then sequentially place the trident-staff in its own form, divided into two parts, upon his left foot.

Having placed the skull that has fallen at its end, one should again place the illuminator of the mantra preceded by the ear-ornament (the letter *u*), joined with the vital drop (*praṇabindu*). ||37||
The knower of the ritual procedure should again place the *prāṇa* with the *visarga*; then, having again placed the left foot, he should place the fallen skull once more.
This Vidyā, known as Parāparā, which bestows all accomplishments and constantly destroys all the sins of men, should be perpetually applied. 39.

But I shall now describe another [method], which bestows the fruit of all desires: having joined the vital breath with the nose, one should remain in the posture of the trident-staff (śūladaṇḍāsana). ||40||
One should first apply the essence of the mantra together with its own vowel; then one should place that very same [essence] conjoined with the *bindu* and joined with the letter *ū*. ||41||
Placing the left foot down again, the skull falls once more; this other [form] is proclaimed as the mighty power of Rudra.
One should always recite with effort for the sake of accomplishing one's desired aims; thereafter, hear about the supreme, most secret, subtle power of Rudra. 43.

This should not be given to one who has not been initiated, nor to one who lacks self-restraint, nor to one who is fearful; [one should not give] Rudra, the power of Rudra, and the Guru, who are indeed non-dual. 44.
O fair-faced one, he who gazes [upon the teacher] with devotion—then, when the guru has been satisfied, even a disciple should receive [the initiation]. (45)

Having formed [the letters] with *daṇḍas*, having formed the excellent *daṇḍa* (the form of the excellent *daṇḍa*), at its end they vanish; first, the *prāṇa* vanishes, then the *prāṇa*, then the *bindu*, and finally the *bindu* with the *visarga*.

Another [mantra] bestows the supreme; one should offer salutations joined with the *praṇava*. Seated upon a throne, accompanied by the teeth (the phonemes), together with that reality (*tattva*), the power of reality (*tattvabala*), for the sake of perfect accomplishment (*saṃsiddhi*)—in the perfected night (*niśisiddhi*)—it is more secret than the secret, subtler than the subtle. To the fearful, it is most terrifying; to the teacher (*guru*), it is the teacher of teachers, conceived as the un-conceived. One should cause the disciple to behold it, and having been satisfied by the disciple, and likewise by the teacher, then, out of discipline, that very Self (*ātman*), conjoined with the left leg, should be given to the disciple. 46.
O Goddess, for one who knows the samaya, this accomplishment that brings forth the fruit of all desires will certainly arise within seven days through this practice. (47)
By the mere knowledge of this Vidyā, she is known through all her powers; or even by its recitation at that very moment, conviction arises in this regard. ||48||
The physical body trembles and likewise leaps up swiftly; it produces various kinds of wealth according to the Siddhayogeśvarīmata. 49.
And for one who, being diligent, recites with devotion these salutations, an immersion [of the deity] arises in his body within a hundred measures (mātrās). ||50||
Whoever remembers for even a moment the Siddhayogeśvarīmata will certainly then bind the supreme collection of mantras and mudrās. ||51||
He will certainly cause the supreme true nature of the scriptures to be grasped; when questioned, he will explain matters pertaining to the past and the future. //52//
This has been told to you in brief, which produces conviction in oneself; thus has the Siddhayogeśvarīmata been explained to you. 53.
O Goddess, these three powers have been described as bestowing divine accomplishments; they are the heart of all powers and are perfected through Aghoreśī. 54.
May there be the *Mālinīvijayottara*.

But that man who remembers for even a moment [the mantra] sealed by the *cumbaka*, he then binds the entire multitude of mantras and mudrās. There is no doubt that there are many ways of binding mudrās taught in the scriptures, such as the *Parātriṃśikā*, the *Tantrasadbhava*, and the *Mālinīvijayottara*: "The binding of mudrās, songs, and even the wailing of Śiva. [Through this practice] the knowledge of the meaning of all scriptures arises in him spontaneously (*akasmāt*), according to the *Mālinīvijayottara*. When questioned, he also recounts past and future events, according to the *Parātriṃśikā* and the *Mālinīvijayottara*: "He should perform the narration and so forth of past and future matters," and "They indeed tell [the truth] when asked about what has been, what is, and what will be," according to the *Tantrasadbhava*. In that [state], for the sake of the disciple... (correction: *tasmiñ śiṣyāya*)... it should be given (*deyaḥ*)... (variant: *vāma* / *vāmam*; correction: *yuktaḥ* / *yuktam*). By this, success (*siddhiḥ*) is attained; (variant: *manasā siddhaḥ* / *manasā siddhāḥ*). At the rising of [the power], for one who knows the *samaya*, after seven days... (variant: *jñātaḥ* / *jñānam*). From its utterance at that very moment, he rises up (*utpatate* / *utpadyate*). O *Yogeśvarī*, wealth (*vittam* / *cittam*) [is attained]. He who is intent upon it... (variant: *yaḥ sam* / *yasyam*). He causes [the disciple] to grasp it (*udgrāhayati* / *udgahayati*), according to the *Tantrasadbhava*. [I have told you] the matter (*arthaḥ* / *arthān*) to you, O *Yogeśvarī*. Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the five limbs of the *vidyā* which are perfected, by which the practitioner of mantra (*mantrī*), being well protected, is not overcome by the lords of obstacles (*vighneśaiḥ*). (Verse 1)

First, the characteristics of the syllables as they have been taught are counted according to the number of *takṣa* [syllables]; the *jaṅghā* (shank), located on the right and accompanied by the nasal dot (*bindu*), is multiplied fivefold. ||2||
"To the heart, obeisance"—this is the supreme heart of the powers; first is the word "Om," and immediately after that, the word "Amṛte. (3)
The word *tejomālinī* followed by *svāhākāra* is thus remembered; this is declared to be the head-mantra (*śiras*), consisting of eleven syllables. ||4||
O fair-faced one, the eight-syllable *śikhā* mantra of the entire host of vidyās should be known as beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ), followed by *vedavedini hūṃ phaṭ*. ||5||
"O Vajrin," and so forth, joined with "to the Vajradhara," beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *svāhā*—this is proclaimed to be the armor-mantra (*varma*). ||6||
O Goddess, one who now recites this eleven-syllable mantra is liberated from elephantiasis and the stigma of being called a "beast"; it is proclaimed to end with *hūm phaṭ*. ||7||
Joined with the *praṇava*, it is remembered as the most excellent of all weapons; known as the six-syllabled mantra, one should cause one's own body to expand [with its power]. ||8||
Stationed within the array of weapons that are the three protectors, this fivefold limb of knowledge indeed crushes all obstacles and tears asunder every hindrance. ||9||

cf. *Mālinīvijayottara* = *Tantrāloka*: "With five *oṃ*s, the mantra becomes the *vidyāṅga-hṛdaya*. cf. *Mālinīvijayottara* = *Tantrāloka*: "Adorned with the words *om amṛte tejomālini svāhā*, this eleven-syllable [mantra] is declared, O Dear One, to be the *brahmaśiras*. cf. *Mālinīvijayottara*: "Endowed with *praṇava* (*oṃ*) at the beginning, followed by *vedavedini huṃ phaṭ*, the eight-syllable *rudrāṇī* is to be known as the *śikhā* of the group of *vidyās*. cf. *Tantrāloka*: "Beginning with *praṇava* and ending with *svāhā*, the eleven-syllable *vajrine vajradharāya svāhā* is remembered as the highly praised *varma* (armor). cf. *Mālinīvijayottara*: "Beginning with *bhava* and ending with *huṃ phaṭ*, the supreme seven-and-a-half syllable *pāśupata* is declared as *ślīpada* and *paśuśabda*. [Textual variants and corrections follow: *Samraksito* (D), *samraksitā* (N); *vighneśair* (conj.), *vighnase* (D), *uddiṣṭā* (D), *uddiṣṭo* (N); *lakṣaṇam* (D), *lakṣaṇam* (N); *dakṣiṇasthā* (em.), *dakṣiṇasyā* (DN); *sabindukā* (codd.), *sabindukāḥ* (DN); *etat* (corr.), *eta* (DN); *tejo* (em.), *teja* (DN); *kāraḥ* (corr.), *kārāt* (DN); *vedavedini huṃ* (suppl., cf. *Mālinīvijayottara*); *vajrinetyādi* (conj., cf. *Mālinīvijayottara*), *vajriṇinyādi* (D), *vajriṇītyādi* (N); *samyuktam* (N), *sammuktam* (D); *varmam* (conj., cf. *Mālinīvijayottara*), *vam* (D), *valam* (N); *sampratam* (D), *saṃvratam* (N); *tvām* (em.), *tvam* (DN); *paśuśabdaḥ* (N), *phaṭāntam* (N), *vṛttayet* (N); *vaśavdan* (D), *huṃ* (D), *hum* (N); *phaḍantam* (corr.), *phaḍāntam* (D), *akṣaram* (D), *ākṣaram* (N); *deham* (corr.), *dehe* (DN); *vṛṃhayet* (D), *seva* (D), *sarva* (N); *stham* (D), *sthau* (N); *hy etat* (N), *-e-m* (D). **PAṬALA** The Goddess said: "O Lord, the three powers (*śaktitraya*) have been described, as well as the five limbs of the *vidyā*. Briefly tell me the treasury of mantras (*mantrakoṣa*) of the world-protectors (*lokapālas*). (1)
Bhairava said: Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the guardians of the world in brief, by means of which one established upon the sacrificial ground attains perfection.
Having first established Indra in the east, one should worship his body on the left breast; then one should worship Agni in the southeast, who bears the form of a trident and a staff.

The skull has Yama as its presiding deity; one should employ it in that [rite]. Furthermore, at the southwest (nairṛta) direction, the navel is proclaimed to have the King of Rākṣasas as its presiding deity. ||4||
Having established Varuṇa, whose form is the throat, in the western direction, the wise man should worship Varuṇa, who possesses great strength and prowess. ||5||
Then, in the northwest, the knower of mantras should likewise worship Vāyu; the mantra for his left shoulder-peak is proclaimed as follows.
Then, having worshipped Soma situated in the north with an ornament placed upon his right ear, he is always beneficial for nourishment.
O lady of beautiful hips, the knower of mantras should always worship Īśāna, who resides on the hip and is situated in the direction of Śaṅkara, that is, the region of Rudra. 8.
One should worship him who has arisen from a golden stalk with his limbs clearly manifest—Mādhava, who stands upon the upper path and is situated below as well. 9.
That which has entered the sense-faculty of smell is the limb devoted to the limbs; it is joined with the mouth, nose, and so forth, and is endowed with that which resides in the secret place. ||10||
Thus the world-protectors (lokapālas) are proclaimed; they have short weapons, measure nine cubits, and should be worshipped according to the rule and with diligence. ||11||

cf. "One should visualize Indra and the others with the long vowels *la*, *ra*, *ṭa*, *kṣa*, *va*, and *ya*, joined with [the consonants] and accompanied by the bindu" (*Mālinīvijayottara*); cf. "In the same way, Viṣṇu and Prajāpati are to be visualized with the nose [vowel *ū*] and the water [vowel *o*]."

The first and third vowels, however, are the designators of the lotus and the wheel (*Mālinīvijayottara* cf. *Mālinīvijayottara* a-c). "The wise one should fashion Indra and the others with short [vowels]; then their weapons" (*Mālinīvijayottara*). *Koṣam* (emended from *koṣa*); *D*: *kāmaṇ*. *Siddhim* (emended from *siddhi*); *D*: *siddhi*. "In brief, [the worship] of the world-protectors... (*N*); *D*: *nāmnākapālādyam*. *Loka* (*N*); *D*: *pālān*. *Pālās* (emended from *pālān*); *N*: *-h*. *D*. "Success" (*N*); *la D*. "Abiding" (emended from *pūrva*); *N*. *Cendram*: *mantra* (*N*). *Tanuḥ*. "In the southeast" (*āgneyyām*); *N*: *āgneyyām*. "With the syllable *adhyayā*, [one places] *Dhara*... "In the southwest, *nnābhī rājaḥ*... "In the direction of sovereignty (*rājya*), having established Varuṇa in the throat, with two forms, in the northwest... *dvāyum vāpu*... "By means of the ornament situated in the right ear, and likewise in the ear... then, in the initiation (*āḍhyāpane*), standing at the waist... standing, *īśānam*... gone, that *mādhavam*... standing in the nourishment (*āpyāyane*)... *gb*... manifest (*vyakta*)... and the path of the subtle body (*tan-mārga*)... the supreme limb below the limbs... endowed with the nose and so forth, they become weapons; nine weapons, extending seven cubits, are to be worshipped according to the injunction. **Patala** Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the accomplished *samayamaṇḍala*, by which authority in this mantra arises, O fair-faced one. (1)
In a place with a single linga, or in a cremation ground, or at the auspicious confluence of two rivers, or on the beautiful shore of the ocean, or again on a mountain peak. ||2||
In a well-concealed shelter, or at a single beautiful tree, in a temple of the Mothers, or in a garden—wherever the mind finds delight. ||3||
Having fasted for a day and night, the Guru, being well-pleased, pure, clad in variegated garments, and purified, shall be equipped with the form of Śakti. ||4||

Having made a portion of ground level, pure, smeared with cow dung, sloping toward the northeast, smooth, and free from husks, charcoal, and bones, one should first examine the site and thereafter begin the consecration. ||5||

He who knows the purification of the place, the purification of the ritual substances, and likewise the purification of the elements, being himself pure, is the Guru who bestows all accomplishments. 6.

Then, having performed the binding of the directions, one should purify [the site] with the weapon-mantra itself; thus the purification of the place is accomplished. Now hear about the supreme purification of the materials. ||7||
O illustrious lady, having washed the *argha* vessel with the *astra* mantra and having thus purified it, one should contemplate the five groups (*varga*). ||8||
One should sprinkle all materials that have been prepared for the sake of the sacrifice; this is declared to be the purification of materials, which increases merit and is never-failing. ||9||

Having further recited the five limbs, one should prepare the five products of the cow (pañcagavya); then, one should smear the ground again and scatter sesame seeds with the weapon-mantra (astra). ||10||

The practitioner should perform the cleansing of the armor (*kavaca*) with a peacock feather; then, the wise one should sprinkle scented water consecrated with the *astra* mantra. By this, the commitment (*samaya*) is established within the mantra. At this time, whether by a river, at the ocean, in the house of a mother-goddess (*mātṛ*), in a garden, or wherever the mind finds pleasure, the practitioner—having fasted for a day and night, being armored, pure, and having smeared his body with ashes—should wash himself thoroughly with the *astra* mantra. Having purified the ground, O Goddess, he should contemplate the purity of the syllables (*varga-śuddhi*) while reciting the mantra over cow products and water with the peacock feather; thus the wise one should cause the purification to be performed.
There, having drawn a square mandala three cubits in size, white in color and with four doors, using either ashes or flour; ||12||
With white, yellow, reddish, and black—these four captivating colors—and with divisions of white, reddish, yellow, and black. ||13||
In its center, one should draw a trident measuring one cubit in size, and one should likewise fashion its shaft as being two cubits long.
To the east of the western door, leaving a space of four finger-breadths, the measurement of the trident-prong is stated here to be equal to the measurement of the door. ||15||
Alternatively, having installed [the image] facing east—measuring one cubit or equal to the span of the belly, which is praised for all rites—it bestows the desired object through its mudrā. ||16||
Placing the little finger on the head, the three [other fingers] straightened, while the index, middle, and ring fingers are extended in the form of horns. ||17||
This auspicious Śūlamudrā, which performs all rites, has been taught by me; like the Jyeṣṭhā peak of Mount Trikūṭa, this Śūlamudrā possesses great power. ||18||
There, on the tip of the trident to the south, one should place the goddess Parāparā, along with the thirty-eight phonemes, resembling a blazing fire.
Adorned with a garland of skulls, radiant with three eyes, holding a trident and a khaṭvāṅga staff, and seated upon a great corpse. ||20||
With a tongue like lightning, a massive body, and adorned with great serpents; she is formidable, possessing large fangs, most fierce, and with eyes knit in a frown. ||21||

She was entwined by great serpents, adorned with a garland of corpses, having beautiful earrings made from the lotus-like hands of great corpses, possessing a roar like the clouds at the end of an aeon, and appearing as if she were swallowing the sky.
*Mālinīvijayottara*: *Mālinīvijayottara* (cf. the *Mālinīvijayottaratantra*). [The fingers] of the right hand—the index, middle, and ring fingers—are extended.

The *triśūla* (trident) is proclaimed as that which is pressed by the little finger and the thumb. At the base of the pericarp (*karṇikā*) is the Lord of the *Mālinīvijaya*, known as the "Always-Designated One" (*sadākhya*), having the form of a *preta*. [He is] formidable, with great fangs, most fierce, and with a face of knitted brows. [She is] formidable, very terrifying, adorned with a garland of corpses. The wise one performs the purification of the ground with sacrifices, [using] reddish, black, and four-colored [substances]. *Tantrāloka*; *Mālinīvijayottara*; *Tantrasadbhāva*; *bhūmiṃ śodhanam* (purification of the ground); *prājñaḥ* (the wise one); *yajñaiḥ* (with sacrifices); *āruṇaiḥ* (reddish); *kṛṣṇaiḥ* (black); *caturvarṇaiḥ* (four-colored). Cf. [references].

O Puṣkaraparameśvara, [the goddess] is described as having bonds for the eyes, with three doors measured from back to back; she is risen, her belly is equal and praised, desired, marked, straight, and the three are upright; she is in the middle, the three peaks are lofty and beautiful in form; she is said to be auspicious, with a trident and a palm, beautiful, the eldest, powerful with a trident and a palm; at the tip, she is both supreme and non-supreme, thirty-eight parts, resembling them; she holds a *khaṭvāṅga* staff, a seat, fangs, a frown, and is encircled by serpents; she holds a lotus, wears a garment and a garland, possesses such a form, and is the goddess who destroys the suffering of those who bow to her; one should again place the other three-syllabled [mantra] on the left tip of the trident.
In this context, the left is indeed the right, and the right is traditionally known as the north; by way of its supreme and inferior forms, this Vidyā is Kṛṣṇapiṅgalā.
One should place the auspicious Goddess, who consists of all syllables, in the center; she shines like ten thousand shimmering suns, illuminating this entire world. ||25||
One should place an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp at the tip of her crest-lock; upon the pericarp, one should place the supreme, auspicious, single-syllabled Goddess.
Resembling the finest crystal, flowing with nectar on all sides, the goddess who provides nourishment and bestows supreme accomplishment. 27.

Having placed [the deities] on the eastern leaf and so forth, one should then invoke the group beginning with Aghorī by means of exhalation (recaka), and restrain them by means of retention (kumbhaka). ||28||

Having worshipped Śiva—the subtle, partless one whose form is the abode—one should perform the ritual dismissal (visarjana) by means of the inhalation (pūraka), through absorption into the Supreme Brahman. ||29||

Having performed the placement of those [syllables] mentioned in the previous mantra, one should then arrange the limbs: one should place the heart in the southeast corner and the head in the northeast.
Having placed the crest-lock (śikhā) in the southwest, one should place the armor (kavaca) in the northwest; the weapon (astra) should be diligently applied in all directions. ||31||

One should indeed place Śakra and the other world-protectors in their own respective positions; this is declared to be the placement of meditation (dhyānanyāsa), which is complete, O fair-faced one. (32)
Then, with flowers, perfumes, lamps, incense, purifiers, garments, jewels, and so forth, one should worship it with devotion according to the prescribed ritual. ||33||
With various kinds of food offerings from all social classes, with archways adorned with banners, and with canopies covering the sky.

With sacrificial pap (caru) esteemed as great meat and excellent wine, one should worship the Goddess who assumes forms at will and destroys the suffering of those who bow before her. On the left horn [of the triangle], however, one should place the other [form], the terrifying, dark-brown goddess. At the tip of her crest, one should place the supreme, auspicious single-syllable [mantra]. The supreme Mother-goddess Mātṛkā is indeed proclaimed to be Mālinī in the center. (Tantrāloka, cf.)

One who knows the ritual procedure should worship with devotion that supreme, nourishing Goddess, who possesses the radiance of ten thousand moons, using perfumes, flowers, lamps, incense, sacred threads, garments, jewels, and other offerings. The three-syllabled [mantra] is the lower (aparā), while the supreme (parā) is also three-syllabled. Vāmā exists in the form of Vāmā, and Arūpā exists as Arūpā; Piṅgalā is not Piṅgalā, and she resides in the middle channel. Of those [channels], the supreme is higher than the highest, most excellent, and the bestower of the supreme state. One should invoke her into Śivā, the partless one, through placement and inhalation, according to the mantra previously taught. Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the Agneyī [weapon] in the southeast, the Śikhā [crown] in the southwest, and the Kavaca [armor]—the first of all—in their respective places, one should worship them with offerings and hymns of praise. Having worshipped with devotion according to the rule, one should offer oneself. *Ślokas 34–35*
Having performed circumambulation there and prostrated with devotion, he should then cause the disciple—who is pure, bathed, and having fasted—to enter. (36)

O Great Goddess, one should give the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) along with kuśa grass to him; having drunk it and performed the ritual rinsing (ācamana) with diligence, one should then begin the consecration (saṃskāra). ||37||
The Guru, having adorned the disciple with perfumes, garlands, garments, incense, and purifying threads, should sprinkle him with water that embodies the mantra.
Then, O Goddess, one should contemplate the disciple being consumed by the heart; once he is completely burnt away, one should contemplate him as having the body of Śakti.
One should again visualize the Goddess consisting of all syllables within his body; then, having performed the placement of the three Vidyās, he is armored with the Heart-mantra and the others.
Then, holding a handful of flowers, the preceptor, being well-composed, should touch his eyes with a white cloth.
Then the knower of mantras should cause the disciples to enter through the western door; having made them bow down at the level of the knees, he should have them perform the casting of flowers.
For whichever [deity] flowers are seen fallen on the tips of the horns, one should assign that deity's name as the first part, ending with the word *śakti*.
Having gathered the disciples once more, the Guru should perform a circumambulation; afterwards, having prostrated and sat down, he should cause them to hear the pledges (samayas).

One must never eat without having first offered [the food] to the Goddess and to me. Having thus worshipped on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), as well as in the water-pot (*kalaśa*), the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*), and in one's own body, one should worship the Supreme Lord after having diligently summoned Him who has become manifest in form. Then, one should cast a flower; wherever that flower falls, there resides His Śakti in His hand. One should discern the lineage (*kula*) of whichever mantra the fallen flowers belong to.
One should observe his clan by means of that name preceded by [the syllable] *Śakti* where the flower falls;
then, having performed a circumambulation of the mandala and having prostrated before the fire,
the preceptor, together with the sacrificial victim, stands near the fire-pit.
Once permitted and consecrated, the Guru should cause him to hear the pledges (samayas). Having caused that disciple,
who has been made to partake of a portion of Rudra, to hear the pledges, the wise Guru should always perform worship of the gods, the fire, the Guru, and the Goddesses.
Without having first offered these [oblations], one should not consume anything at all.

Having prostrated according to the rule, one should contemplate those who have fasted as being endowed with garlands; then, having visualized their bodies as burnt away by power, one should strike them while they are armored.
Having seen those disciples through the door, one should circumambulate the disciples clockwise as far as the power-limit (śaktyanta);
thereafter, having sat down, one should eat only after making the offering. Never otherwise.
One should not revile a woman, a scripture, wine, a eunuch, or even a young girl.
One should never exert oneself in what is fruitless, nor should one take food according to an improper method;
one should never, at any time, utter the sound "rere."
A wise man should not eat anything from the leaves of the banyan, the holy fig tree, or the sun plant; he should not look at a naked woman, nor even at one who is partially naked.
One who desires accomplishment during the day should not watch animal sports, should not perform base actions, and should always avoid sexual intercourse with village women.
Having consecrated one's own body through the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, one should contemplate one's power throughout the three periods of the day;
one should honor the preceptor who is nearby, and the one who is far away through the yoga of meditation.
Likewise, one should avoid meat produced from camels, owls, buffaloes, and female jackals; one should completely avoid the flesh of bears, chickens, and peacocks.
One should not speak of "ḍākinī" even to practitioners out of negligence,
whether at sacred fields, on paths, under solitary trees, or in cremation grounds and shrines.

One should not despise anyone who is deformed, suffering, impotent, eunuch, or afflicted by thirst... O beautiful woman, a wise man should never revile a maiden, nor ever loathe the heroic substances [used] for intoxication;
rather, he should praise them, always delight in them, and constantly worship the young girl.
One should not criticize the Lord, nor the speech arising from Him;
one should avoid fruitless exertion and perform no vain action; one should not perform a useless rite, nor eat meat contrary to the rules;
and one should never eat from the leaves of the *vaṭa*, *aśvattha*, or *arka* trees.
One should not do anything toward women by which one might be held in contempt by them.
Therefore, one should not look at naked women, nor at those whose breasts are exposed; (cf.

*na nagnām vīkṣayed rāmām nagnām nekṣeta ca striyam* = "One should not look at a beautiful woman when she is naked, nor should one look at a naked woman"). One should not observe animal sports, nor should one cause minor, vulgar acts to be performed.
One who desires success should not engage in worldly village-duties during the day;
one should worship the God three times a day,
just as one would always worship a Guru whether he is staying or departing.
Since, through his grace, one may attain all forms of prosperity,
therefore one should worship the guru with effort, as if he were Mahādeva himself.
Indeed, always with devotion, affection, effort, and faith—
[one should offer] a bull, a cock, a peacock, a swan, and likewise a boar, a buffalo, a human, a monitor lizard, an owl, a vulture, and a hawk.
The flesh of goats, deer, sheep, dogs, jackals, rabbits, and porcupines, as well as that of any other animals which is considered loathsome even in thought, must not be eaten;
one should not refer to such meat as "meat of the *śākinī*."

One should never utter a word denoting a *śākinī*, nor should one utter the sounds "he-he" or "he-i. A wise man, O beautiful lady, should not revile or abuse another who is deformed, suffering, mute, impotent, or afflicted by thirst; he should not speak ill of a maiden.

One should not revile one who is deformed, suffering, impotent, emasculated, or another afflicted by thirst... nor, O beautiful woman, should one revile a woman, a scripture, wine, or a maiden that is fruitless. According to the *Mālinīvijayottara*, one should never employ what is not to be taken according to the rule, nor what is to be taken without the rule; one desiring dharma should never look upon a naked woman with exposed breasts in the open water.

One should contemplate power at the three times of day; one should pay homage to the power of consciousness. [The mantra is: *olūka olva olva*, *mahisi mahisīm mahirsi jam*, *tam*, *ṛkṣa rikṣa kukkuta kurkkuta*, *māyūra māyūram*, *dākinī dagini*. The knower of mantras should never void excrement or urine, nor sleep, under a solitary tree by the road, or in a temple that is solitary. Having thus caused [the disciple] to hear these and other pledges (*samaya*), then the Guru— (52)
With devotion and a concentrated mind, one should perform the ritual withdrawal using one's own mantras;
then, having completed all that, one should cast the food offering into the water. ||53||
Thus has this maṇḍala been proclaimed as the pledge for those who seek the pledge; O Goddess, by the mere sight of which eternal accomplishment is attained. ||54||
Having carefully drawn the arrangement of the initiation mandala, accompanied by the group of eight beginning with Aghorī, within the cremation grounds or the sacrificial enclosures; 55.

There, having worshipped the Lord of Gods, Bhairava, who is the embodiment of mantra, one should perform eight oblations with the reversed [mantra]; O Maheśānī, if one is capable, one should offer a hundred [oblations] in sequence, beginning with Aghorī and the rest of the eight. 56.
For one who has been consecrated and authorized in the maṇḍala of the Siddhayogeśvarīs shall, before long, proceed to the state that transcends the station of all powers. ||57||
One must never sleep under a single tree or at a crossroads.
One should never void urine or excrement, nor spit, nor engage in sexual intercourse in a field, a cremation ground, a forest, or groves;
nor in a temple, on a riverbank, or amidst ashes and cow dung. One should not urinate on a path, nor in ashes, nor in a cow-pen.
"Neither on ploughed ground, nor in water, nor on a funeral pyre, nor on a mountain, nor in a ruined temple, nor ever on an anthill"—
having thus caused [the disciple] to hear such pledges (*samaya*), he should dismiss him.

Having thus proclaimed the pledges (*samaya*) and worshipped the deity, the instructor (*daiśika*) should partake of the food offering (*naivedya*) by the river and cast its remains into the water. Those who have been initiated into each respective principle (*tattva*) by means of eight oblations (*ahuti*) are joined to the rite of initiation through these eight oblations. For the purpose of purifying the site, the practitioner of mantras (*mantrī*) should offer one hundred and eight oblations for each [principle]; thus the purification of the site is accomplished. Then, having summoned [the deities] according to this procedure and with their respective mantras, following the method of the previous sūtra, by means of the eight [deities] beginning with Aghorī.

Or, O Goddess, by means of the three powers (śakti), there is the complete purification of all [the goddesses]. [One should cast] urine (mūtra), the bed of urine (mūtra-śayana), the bed (śayana), the observance (samaya), the observance (samaya), the withdrawal (upasamhāra), the withdrawal (upasamghāra), the dwelling (kṣipet), the dwelling (kṣiyet), the beholding (samdarśane), the beholding (sadarśana), the beholding (samdaśane), success (siddhir), success (siddhimr), success (siddhim), Aghorī and the other eight [goddesses], Aghorī and the others, Aghorī and so forth; in the winds (vāteṣu), in the winds (vāteṣu), the group of eight (astaka), the group of eight (āṣṭaka); by the reverse (viparītena), by the reverse (viparītana), the power (śakto), the power (śaktā), O Maheśānī, O Mahāsānī, the group of eight (astakam), the group of eight (aṣṭakā). Being authorized (anujñātaḥ), being authorized (anujñāta), O Lord of Yogins (yogeśa), O King of Yogins (yogīsa), one quickly [attains] all powers (sarvaśaktīnām), quickly [all] powers (savvabhaktīnām).
Bhairava said:
Now follows this rule of conduct for the great-souled practitioner. ||1||

One who knows the ritual procedure, standing in the southern direction after having worshipped the Goddess according to the prescribed arrangement, should perform the initiation that grants all perfections to men. ||2||
When that [liṅga] has been struck with ashes while facing north, one should wash it with water consecrated by the recitation of the King of Mantras (astrarāja). ||3||
When this has been done, the wise practitioner should then perform the ritual placement (nyāsa); thereafter, he should offer the sacred thread (pavitraka) consecrated with the Rudrāṇī mantra.
Then, the knower of mantras should perform this rite upon the disciple with fragrant flowers, incense, and the water-offering (arghya) and so forth, in due order, using his own mantra alone. ||5||

Then, standing near the fire and facing the directions beginning with the north (Saumya), he should perform the initiation upon the body of the bound soul (paśu) which has been struck with kuśa grass and other implements.
O beloved, both Prakṛti and Puruṣa, as well as Śiva himself, are threefold; everything is pure through these pure [principles], so no further deliberation is required here. ||7||
O fair-faced one, one should first purify Pradhāna by means of the three-syllabled mantra, and thereafter the Puruṣa, the twenty-fifth principle, by means of the Parāparā mantra. (8)
Thereafter, the knower of the ritual procedure should purify the mantra-body as it is established, and he should then unite it with the stainless Parā.

Then one should fashion the locus, and thereafter again perform the placement of the womb (yoninyāsa); then the grasping and the conjunction, and from that one should generate the practitioner (sādhaka). ||10||

O Dear One, authority (*adhikāra*), enjoyment (*bhoga*), and dissolution (*laya*) are likewise threefold. On the right side of the abode (*dhāman*) is the "Southern" (*dakṣiṇa*); it is so called because it burns away the bonds (*pāśaploṣakatva*) of the one facing south (*dākṣiṇāsyasya*). Having sprinkled the disciple with the Weapon-mantra (*astra*), he should dissolve [the bonds] while reciting the Weapon-mantra. Sprinkling is performed according to the region of the heart; [it is said that] Śivā is in the thread of the bonds (*pāśasūtre*). As for the striking (*tāḍana*), it is done with ashes or with those very [materials]. Having struck with the water of Śiva and with ashes and *kuśa*-grass in sequence, the phrase "with the Weapon-mantra" (*astreṇa*) is to be applied to all three.

The seizing (*grahaṇa*), the joining (*yojana*), and the separation (*viyoga*) should be performed by the wise in due order through the ritual procedure seen in the scriptures. One should perform the seizing, the joining, as well as the separation, the extraction, and whatever [rites] such as the cutting of the noose (*pāśaccheda*) [are required]. Having seized him at the heart with the hand of Śiva, the learned one should again perform his seizing by means of the non-separation from the measure of the rays (*raśmimātrā*).

Having traveled by way of the channels (*nāḍī*) and having placed [the seed] within himself using the *hṛdaya* and *mantra-puṭita* [mantras], the wise practitioner of mantra should then contemplate the impregnation (*garbhādhāna*) in the womb, accompanied by all the rites of gestation, through the perfection of the capacity for being the enjoyer and the enjoyed. (Kṣemarāja ad loc.)

Now, this and this [is the procedure]: one who knows the rule of initiation (*dīkṣā*) should perform the initiation; the knower of the rule, having sacrificed with the *karī* and *karī* [mantras] here and there, should wash away the sacrifice performed with the weapon-mantra (*astra*) by means of the recited mantra. Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*), the knower should destroy the impurity (*nāśam*) by means of the *pavitraka* mantra, O *pavitraka*, through the mantra of Rudrāṇī. Standing as a knower, gentle and so forth, he should strike with *kuśa* grass and other materials beginning with the letter *ta*. Having struck the body in its form, these pure [elements] should be purified for the sake of the higher and lower [state]. The body should be joined to the stainless one; then, having struck with those beginning with *ta*, everything should be purified with the *ima* mantras. Then, in the *parā* [state], the knower should purify and fashion the stainless [state]; then he should effect enjoyment (*bhoga*) and the severing of bonds (*pāśaccheda*), and likewise the assignment to the proper place. ||11||
Then, having performed those very rites with three oblations, one should likewise effect the purification of the site with one hundred and eight [oblations].
But when there is a cause for expiation, the mantra-practitioner should offer oblations according to the number of animals and should recollect the King of Weapons (astra). ||13||
Then the wise one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with his own mantra; in this sequence, he should thus purify the remainder for the practitioner.
Whether in the state of Sakala or even in Laya, one should then perform the ritual action; subsequently, one should unite the supreme practitioner with either the Sakala or the Niṣkala state.

O fair-faced one, for one desiring supernatural powers (*siddhi*), the wise practitioner should perform yoga with the *parā* [form] in its entirety; for one desiring liberation, he should do so with the partless (*niṣkala*) form. ||16||

Then, having thus become initiated, one who desires accomplishment and is composed should subsequently perform the reception of that [teaching], after having honored the preceptor according to his own capacity. ||17||
One should offer oneself to the guru with a threefold inner disposition; thereafter, the wise one should request: "What should be done after this? (18)
Whatever has been commanded by him must indeed be accomplished exactly so; one should perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa as it has been described, O fair-faced one. (19)

One's own body should be purified by means of the supreme [method] through three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma): having exhaled the air from one's own body, one should draw it back in again and retain it. ||20||

When one is not released from the retention (kumbhaka) by means of the supreme seed-syllable, one should maintain the supreme [state] together with tranquility; this is remembered as the fourth, the mental [state]. ||21||
Having thus purified one's own body through diligent practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should then install the Goddess, who is endowed with all phonemes, within that body. 22.

One's hands should first be purified with the *parā* mantra, and likewise with the *aparā*; one should always perform the purification of the directions (*dikśuddhi*) at the beginning with the *astra* mantra, while the binding of the quarters (*āśābandha*) is recommended to be performed according to the rule with the *varma* mantra. (23)
Thereafter, one should always meditate upon the Goddess Parāparā within the lotus of the heart, seated upon the pericarp in her own form. ||24||

In the same way, one should perform the placement of the other [mantras] at the region of the head; that [first mantra] is above the pericarp, while the other vidyā, pertaining to the triad of vidyās, extends from the feet upward. 25.
Aghorā, Paramāghorā, Ghorarūpā, and another, Ghorāsyā, Parāguhyā, Bhīmā, and Bhīṣaṇā are the leaders. ||26||

One [mudrā] is for inducing vomiting, another is for delighting in drinking, and yet another drinks; then, having placed [the hands] at the end of the feet, one proceeds in order from the region of the head. ||27||
Furthermore, the accomplished yogi, having diligently understood everything within the body, should arrange the heart and other limbs in their respective locations. || 28 ||
And here, the "Eight Flowers" (aṣṭapuṣpikā) is prescribed by that very same conventional path; and if you so desire, the fire-ritual (agnikārya) is performed with that same arrangement. ||29||

The mere performance of the ritual placement (nyāsa) is fully described as bestowing the enjoyment of yoga within six months; by this alone, the wise achieve perfection in six months, without a doubt. ||30||
O Goddess, when this nyāsa is always performed, it destroys the pride of all who cause harm; O Beloved, I have thus described to you the fivefold [nyāsa] beginning with Mālinī. 31.
Furthermore, the conclusion of the limbs should be performed briefly in five ways; if one recites this at the time of battle, one will undoubtedly attain victory. || 32 ||

The knower of that should contemplate this very question according to its proper arrangement; when it has entered the state of the Parā, Aparā, and Avaktra, he then accomplishes [the goal] in an instant. ||33||
One should mutter the mantra of the supreme goddess, who has blood-red eyes, one hundred and eight times until she makes the [victim] utterly lifeless. ||34||
A stream of formless blood, like an Ashoka tree in full bloom. ||35||

Having thus placed the wheel in her left hand, O Great Goddess, one should imagine that hand placed upon the heart of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*). One should visualize [the wheel] as flowing with divine wine, possessing a luster equal to a hundred thousand tastes. Having remained for a moment in this supreme state, one is then praised by means of armor and the Dharma. Then, by means of one's own lotus, she remains in that very region; and he, through ignorance of his supreme form, is terrified by the fierce and formidable Leader. Another is devoted to drinking and drinks; thus, having known everything from beginning to end, one who is omniscient should remain in his own states as he desires. Measure by measure, through the true praise of the lotus, this yoga is always practiced by the virtuous. Immediately, the placement (*nyāsa*) should be performed by the wise: "All, all, the destroyer, the swan, the remover of pride; O Beloved, may you love me; may the end of the body be ready for the supreme beyond. For a woman, the victory of women is won by the knower of that; from eye to eye, with eyes full of passion, he is devoted to the passionate woman. One should recite the *rakta* mantra eight hundred times—*rakta*, *rakta*, *rākṣaka*—and at that very moment, one brings her under control. When a calamity has arisen, one should apply the white [syllable] to oneself. [Verse 36]
At that very moment, one is liberated from all obstacles; there is no doubt about this. He who remembers the White [Goddess] every day shall attain poetic genius. ||37||
Within one month, the wise man becomes free from other thoughts; within two months, he attains good fortune, being free from other thoughts. ||38||
In three months one attains the nourishment of form; in the fourth, wealth; in the fifth, a divine form; and in the sixth, every desire as wished for. ||39||
Thus, he who performs the mere ritual placement (nyāsa) in this sequence for six months should also perform the recitation (japa) here, consisting of one thousand and eight [repetitions]. ||40||
O lady of excellent hips, for one devoted to the fire-ritual, one should perform meditation in this manner; thereby, happiness is attained. ||41||

Whoever approaches her during an eclipse, she brings them under control in an instant. By means of recitation and study, one’s own form increases month by month. Wealth, arrows, and desire—whatever is desired, whatever is wished for—one attains it through the months of recitation. Those who have reached the ultimate goal, who are devoted to the ultimate goal, should practice in this very manner; they should practice just that much, being devoted to that alone. Chapter 8.
The Goddess said:

"O Lord, I have understood the rule characterized by the reception of the mantra, as well as the arrangement of the initiation mandala accompanied by the eight [deities] beginning with Aghora; yet it has certainly not been indicated or explained through the initiation itself. (1)
O Lord, what was indicated by you has not been clearly explained to me; therefore, O Lord of Gods, speak thus to me for the sake of destroying my doubt.
I wish to know that by which enjoyment and liberation proceed for one who has merely been initiated; O Blessed One, you should deign to speak of this. ||3||
Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, to this supreme secret which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, within this Mahābhairavatantra known as the Siddhayogeśvarīmata. (4)

In a cremation ground, on a plot of land, or even in the house of a mother, one should draw a lotus in the center with half of that [measurement] as the prongs of the trident; these are the [lines of the] mandala. The Goddess said: "O God, you must certainly establish for me the arrangement of the *samaya* (sacred observance) for the sake of the destruction of the gods and for liberation. Bhairava said: "In the portion intended for sacrifice, having examined it according to the ritual, one should strike the portion with the weapon of the gods, and with a mallet, one should pound it. With petals, one should [draw] the enclosure; with eight lotuses, the lotuses; with petals, the petals. According to the measure of half [the size], and in the act of measuring, and in the act of bestowing, the prongs of the trident are increased by the lineage in the corners themselves, and in those very corners, another [element] is known. Having understood this, having drawn the fangs with the seals, his body is made Bhairava-like through the sixfold sequence."
One should worship there in the center Bhairava, who is dear to Bhairavī and the bestower of the siddhis of Bhairavī, situated within the pericarp. 14.

On the eight petals, starting from the eastern petal and proceeding in order, [one should worship] Aghorī and the others, as well as the limbs of the Goddess, the secret [limbs], and then the eight world-protectors (lokapāla). Then, having cleansed [the vessel] with the weapon-mantra according to the rule, one should satisfy [the deities] with sacrificial porridges (caru), as well as those [deities] previously consecrated and for whom the rites of protection have been performed.

Having adorned those whose bodies have been made terrifying with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and having assigned them to Bhairava for the sake of the previous worship, one should cause them to enter the mandala according to the previously stated procedure; then, having summoned them with kuśa grass in their hands, one should commence the initiation. Then, having gone to the fire-pit and standing facing the east, one should perform the preliminary rite there and then prepare the sacrificial vessel (māṃsa).

Having invoked Kṛṣṇarudra, one should contemplate the right calf; having meditated on the right calf as being endowed with a *bindu* and as the [divine] abode in its true form, one should thus perform the visualization of the abode (*sthāna-kalpana*).

Then follows the visualization of the womb (*yoni-vikalpana*), which is joined with one's own eight mantras; having worshipped it in due order with flowers and other offerings, one should then place the *bindu* upon the nose and contemplate the power of Rudra (*rudra-śakti*), worshipping it with fragrant flowers according to the prescribed rite.

There, one should honor the disciples and perform eight oblations; having thus performed the ritual procedure, one should then unite them with the mantra (aṇu). [One should place it] on the left foot, the hip, or else on the knee. The vital breath (prāṇa), mounted upon the staff of the trident and adorned by the nose, joined with the visarga—this one should employ for the purposes of union, application, authority, enjoyment, and dissolution.
Likewise, at the cutting of the noose and at the gate, by means of three oblations each, they are initiated into each *tattva* through the offering of eight oblations.
(26) For the purpose of purifying the locations, the practitioner of mantras should offer one hundred and eight oblations; from that, the purification of the locations is accomplished.
(27) O illustrious lady, this very procedure is to be known as the "universal foundation" (*sarvādhāna*), extending from Kālāgnirudra up to the *tattva* of Śiva. (28)

On the eight petals are Aghorī and the others; indeed, Ghoryā and the others, and likewise those beginning with Ghoryā, who are the limbs of the Goddess. Having cleansed each weapon (*astra*) by sprinkling (*mārjya*, *mājya*, *majya*), one should perform the preceding ritual actions (*vidhikriyā*). Having performed, completed, cast down, and discarded the rites, one should then fashion the hands, the thighs (*jaṅghā*), the *Njaṅghom*, the *Danu*, the *Anum*, and the *Āditam*. Joined with the *Doditam* and the *Yutam*, one should worship with fragrance (*sugandha*, *sugandhi*). Having worshipped the power (*śakti*) from the beginning, and having worshipped the rites (*vidhi*) that are to be worshipped, the eight rites are established. The disciples (*chiṣyān*, *chiṣyām*), the *Anum*, the *Anum*, the conjunction (*samyojana*), the state of conjunction (*samyojanatva*), the authority (*adhikāra*), the enjoyment (*bhoga*), the portion (*bhāga*), the group of eight (*astaka*), and the group of eight divine origins (*devayoni*) have been worshipped in their eightfold manner. ||33||
There are fifty-six supreme secret Mothers by the thousands—those of Māyā, Krodha, Rāga, and likewise those of Kāla.
O you of excellent vows, these seven secret Mothers bestow enjoyment through their ritual placement (*vinyāsa*), follow the station of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), and grant all sovereignty.
Having taken recourse to the principle (*tattva*) of Bhairava, they are the initiators of emanation; the Mothers stationed therein are indeed the Mothers who bestow grace.
O fair-faced one, those [Mothers] who reside in the principles (tattva) of Pradhāna, Rāga, Puruṣa, and Niyati; those situated in Vidyā, Kalā, Kāla, and Māyā;

those established in Īśvara and Sadāśiva; and those established in Śiva, Bhairava, and Guhya—these peaceful Mothers, O highly fortunate lady, are all pure, having been purified respectively by nine, seven, five, and three [principles] in due order. || 37–39 ||

Having summoned [the deities] with their own mantras according to this rite and through yoga—specifically by means of the eight [mantras] beginning with Aghorī following the previous sūtra, or else by means of the triad of Śaktis, O Goddess—the purification of all [the deities] is performed.

For the sake of accomplishing the goal of Bhairavī, the practitioner of mantra should employ [these mantras]. But for the sake of liberation, O Goddess, one should join the bound soul (paśu) to the reality (tattva) of Bhairava.
In the case of the employment of the Parāparā [mantra], one should again employ the Aparā; however, in the case of separation from all the tattvas, the Parā [mantra] brings liberation in an instant.
When employed in the rite of initiation through the offering of eight oblations, and joined with the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), it bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
(43) O fair-faced one, this application of the final oblation should be performed at each and every level of reality (*tattva*).
(44) Regarding the phrase "oblations for the sake of liberation," one should apply them here according to their actual state. (46)
[They] have [placed] their mind on that supreme Siddhayogeśvarī, O Goddess.
||47-48|| Chapter 10. The Goddess said: O Lord, previously I asked about the doctrine of the Siddhayogeśvarīs, which is devoid of vows and sacrifices, yet accomplishes the mantras. ||1||
"But, O Lord, since spiritual accomplishment (*siddhi*) is established as a limb of knowledge (*vidyā*), therefore please tell me in brief the practice of the vow (*vratacaryā*).

Bhairava said: First, for the sake of all accomplishments, for the destruction of all obstacles, and for the removal of all sins, having performed the sacrifice (*yāga*) of the mantra and its deity according to the rule, [one should perform] the practice of the vow."
One should wander alone like an arrow; this is proclaimed as the bestower of success.

[Clad in] yellow garments, [with a frown] drawn, one should laugh with a loud, boisterous laugh (*aṭṭahāsa*). Having performed the practice of reciting the mantra, the forms of Rudrāṇī and the other goddesses are thus manifested. ||8-10||

[Having performed the sacrifice with all-black offerings, one should wander again. The practitioner, for the sake of attaining mantra-perfection (*mantrasiddhi*), should observe the mantra-vow (*mantravrata*). *Mālinīvijayottara* 10.12cd; "Then, protected by these mantras, he shall become peerless; invincible to all wicked beings, strengthened by the splendor of the mantra. *Mālinīvijayottara* 10.16cd–17ab. 4b: "With his mind absorbed in meditation upon that [deity]. *SYM* 13.4b. 5: cf. "Having thus performed what is prescribed for the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), having bathed, one should recite the *Vidyādhipa*. *Mālinīvijayottara* 10.13ab. 6–8: cf. "And having performed the consecration as before, one should recite the *Brahmaśiras*. *Mālinīvijayottara* 10.14ab. 9–10: cf. "And three hundred thousand [recitations] of the *Rudrāṇī*. *Mālinīvijayottara* 10.15a (emend *dvayam* to *trayam* as per edition).
1b *vrata* N; *evam* D. 1c *siddha* D; *siddhi* N.

The mistress of yoga (yogīśvarī), according to the doctrine (mata) of all [beings], is established in accomplishment (siddhi). In brief, this is the conduct (caryā). One who removes evil, a practitioner (sādhaka), or even a hero (vīra), with his mind fixed on that [reality], should perform the sacrifice (yāga) himself. This is the conduct. Having smeared [the ground], wearing the sacred thread (upavīta), and possessing a lower lip [red as] blood, one should wander about. Wearing the sacred thread, laughing loudly, with a single arrow in the mind, he should wander. This is the vow (vrata); it is the head of Brahmā (brahmaśiras). This belongs to him. Yellow, wearing the sacred thread, firm, patient, and with senses restrained—this is the conduct (ācāra) of the god. By means of this conduct, having performed the sacrifice, he shall go. And [he may have] a fierce gaze, frowns, or sometimes threats with words. (11)
One should wander about covered with a black-colored cloth; this is the vow of Puruṣṭuta, which brings subjection and grants the accomplishment of one's goals. || 12 ||
[In some places red, in some yellow, in some black, and in some white]; thus, with various forms, his left hand is likewise raised. || 13 ||
Wearing but a single garment or indeed no garment at all, silent, with his intellect bound by the mantra, he should wander through the village streets as well as in sacred shrines. || 14 ||
One should indeed observe this most formidable vow, whether standing still or walking about; this is called the Pāśupata, which bestows immediate perfection. ||15||
For this threefold vow must be performed for five days; one should recite each of the mantras one hundred thousand times in their proper sequence. ||16||
With the rosary held in the left hand, the practitioner should recite it neither indistinctly, nor with a distracted mind, nor without commitment, nor too rapidly. ||17||
The practitioner should perform such a recitation, which grants all desires, remaining without blinking both at the time of undertaking the vow and at its conclusion. (18)
Having performed the sacrifice according to the rules and bathed with his own water-pot, he shall be liberated from obstacles and thereafter become fit for the mantra. ||19||
Thus, having bathed after the observance of knowledge (vidyāvratasnāta) and being freed from all obstacles, one should offer a most weighty arghya out of a desire for the state of the Yoginīs. ||20||

11ab–12cd: The wise person should observe the vow of Puruṣṭuta for one month, always devoted to the worship of Śiva with all-black offerings. (Svāyambhuvasūtrasaṃgraha 21.32) 11–12: [The mantra] Puruṣṭuta consists of four [syllables]. (Mālinīvijayottara 10.156) 13: [He is] adorned with white, red, yellow, black, and variegated garments and ornaments. (Mālinīvijayottara 10.16ab) 14a: [He may be] clad in a single garment or naked. (Niśvāsamukha ?.92a; cf. Pāśupatasūtra 1.10–11) 15: O Goddess, one should recite the Mahāpāśupata [mantra] five hundred thousand times. (Mālinīvijayottara 10.15cd; cf. Kubjikāmata 25.53a) 17cd: The wise practitioner should perform the recitation without delay, not indistinctly, not with a distorted voice, not too fast, not counting [the repetitions], and without mental distraction. (Svāyambhuvasūtrasaṃgraha 21.28) 19: At the conclusion of the vow, one should consecrate oneself with the water of Śiva from a jar, over which one’s own mantra has been recited. Having thus bathed according to the Vidyā-vow, the sinless one is authorized in all [rites]. Chapter 11 The Goddess said: "O Mahādeva, you have indicated the *Mṛtyuñjaya* [mantra], which removes old age and death for human beings; O God, tell that to me in brief. (1)
Bhairava said: "Excellent, excellent, O Great Goddess! For I have been exhorted by you, and indeed questioned by the Asuras, the gods, the Brahmas, the Śukras, and the Dānavas. (2)
O beloved, listen as I briefly describe Mṛtyuñjaya, the supreme remover of old age and death, for the sake of the welfare of the entire world. 3.
One should meditate on space as the abode of the elements, wherein there is a white lotus-shape endowed with eight petals and situated upon a pericarp. ||4||
Resembling clear crystal, like a ground of frost, divine and consisting entirely of nectar, with its pericarp fashioned from the moon. ||5||
In that very form, he sat upon a beautiful earth-lotus, having performed the proper ritual placement (*nyāsa*). ||6||
Then, having thus contemplated oneself as having the luster of frost and the brilliance of pure crystal, one should subsequently contemplate the meditation. (7)
One should contemplate the supreme goddess, who has the form of fragrance, situated within the pericarp of the moon that resides in the lotus of the sky. 8.
Resembling clear crystal, flowing with nectar on all sides, it pours forth divine nectar that moves along the end of the resonance of mantra. ||9||
That power of the God of gods is indeed supreme and flows with nectar; it streams forth as the highest milk, which is truth and perfectly pure. ||10||
One should contemplate that [nectar] falling upon one's own form from all sides, clearly flooding the interior of the heart-cave through the aperture of Brahma.
Thus, one should meditate daily and recite this most excellent of mantras; the certainty of the scripture is that within six months one conquers death. 12.

And indeed, that river was [guarded] by the Asuras and Dānavas. Resembling crystal, it flowed upon the earth; within that, the moon, possessing the brilliance of snow, remained as the pericarp. Flowing with supreme nectar, it is indeed the essence of clarified butter. Within the form of the seed-syllable, resting in the heart, the Jina is certain. One should recite the mantra, which falls and floats through its power. The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, O Sinless One, how does that poetic power which was previously mentioned by you arise, O God, in the most excellent practitioner? (1)
Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, to this supreme secret that must be guarded with great effort; listen with a one-pointed mind to that by which poetic genius is born. (2)
Having worshipped with diligence the Goddess according to her true form, and having offered oblations into the fire according to the rule, one should subsequently apply oneself to meditation. ||3||
Having meditated upon her as being of supreme nature, seated upon a lotus-throne in the sky, with [her] left hand resting [therein] and consisting of all-encompassing knowledge; ||4||
Then again, O Varārohā, with her right hand she held a book, and with her [other] hand a divine, excellent rosary made of crystal.
Indeed, she wears around her neck a divine garland composed of [flowers] shaped like kadamba buds, bearing flickering rows of flames. ||6||
Reaching down to the feet, it was transparent like crystal on all sides, flowing with divine nectar, and situated in the midst of a grove of kadamba trees.
Then, one should meditate on that very form of oneself as emitting all-knowledge from its own mouth in great torrents.
Having done this, thereafter the supreme practitioner should visualize a great flood of nectar and of scriptures issuing from his own mouth. (9)
In this way one should apply oneself to meditation; then, within just a month, there arises for him the power of poetic composition, beautiful and adorned with literary ornaments. 10.

O Goddess, it is certain that he who explains all meanings will himself become a composer of scriptures within six months; indeed, he becomes one who knows the scriptures in their entirety, as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of his hand. 11.
O Goddess of gods, whatever verbal composition is proclaimed in the world as something to be known—all that belongs to him, both in its wording and in its meaning.

Or else, having entered a very spacious and beautiful cave, one who has attained absorption (*tanmayatā*) should meditate on the letter *Gb*, which possesses a radiant form through the shapes of the hands and crystal, and which vomits the nectar from its throat. Through meditation on that [letter], the destroyer of obstacles becomes a knower of the world within six months;
indeed, having reached a cave that is free from wicked beings, one situated there should begin the recitation (*japa*). (13)
Remaining there, invisible even to other practitioners, the mantra-master should recite the mantra of the goddess Sulakṣaṇā according to the prescribed rite. (14)
Within one month, the sage who observes the vow [of recitation] completes three hundred thousand [recitations], subsisting on fruits, or tubers, or vegetables, or even on parched grain flour. ||15||
Having consumed either milk, curd, or the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) mixed with ghee—whichever one of these it may be—and reciting [the mantra], one becomes Vācaspati. ||16||
His scriptures, the Vedic branches, are themselves remembered as direct perception; furthermore, whatever exists in the form of speech would likewise be direct perception for him. (17)
And his speech shall proceed adorned with poetic ornaments; he shall live for a very long time, free from old age and disease. ||18||
The fortunate one is always honored by all the world like a lord; there is no doubt that they become his obedient servants, ready to do whatever he commands. (19)
Whatever he may do within those two months should be carefully observed; then Śrīrūpa will arrive and enter along with the practitioner.
Then, having enjoyed the earth girt by the seven oceans, he goes from that time forth to whatever place he has conceived in his mind. (21)
Those who are obedient to his commands, residing in whichever continent they may be, and those appointed by him, carry out the administration of the kingdom free from enmity.
In this manner, one should gradually behold the supreme Manonmanī, whose form is Śakti; having seen her and become absorbed in her, one should enter the state free from all affliction. ||23||

With a hundred thousand [recitations] of *su-em*, with *em* and *S* as the characteristics, with *em* and *S* as the stalks, with *D* and *N* as the vegetables, with *Ns* and *ktubhiḥ* as the flour, with *em* and *ghṛtena* as the clarified butter, while reciting, the branches are themselves *em*. The speech is corrected; she is adorned by *corr*; indeed, *N* and *ava* follow.
